projects.title: LeKwarta
projects.summary: An Android finance app styled like a basketball arena: a scoreboard balance, a shot-clock daily budget, a spending heatmap calendar, accounts, yearly box scores, and a live stock watchlist.
projects.content:
LeKwarta (“Your money, your court”) mixes LeBron James with kwarta, Filipino slang for money. It started as an unfinished course prototype that depended on a PHP server running on XAMPP. I finished it: the data now lives on the phone, the planned Accounts and More tabs work, and the whole app got a basketball-arena redesign in Lakers purple and gold.

Features

  • Scoreboard and shot clock: total balance shown like an arena scoreboard, and a ring that fills as you spend against your daily budget, turning red when you go over. A streak counter tracks days under budget.
  • Heatmap calendar: each day is shaded by how much was spent relative to the budget. Tap a day to see and filter its transactions.
  • Transactions: log expenses by category, income, or transfers between accounts, for any past date. Every entry moves money in or out of an account, and deleting one reverses it.
  • Accounts: color-coded wallet cards for cash, banks, and e-wallets that you can add, rename, reset, or delete.
  • Box score: earned, spent, and net for any day, month, or year, with spending by category and a month-by-month chart.
  • Calculator and stocks: simple interest, compound interest, and loan payments, plus a market overview and watchlist with live Finnhub quotes.

How it's built

  • Kotlin with XML layouts and Material Components; a single activity with fragments, the Navigation component, and a bottom navigation bar.
  • An on-device SQLite database (SQLiteOpenHelper) for users, accounts, and transactions. Balance changes run inside database transactions so they can't get out of sync.
  • Local sign-up and login with passwords hashed using PBKDF2, plus a one-tap demo account with sample data.
  • The shot clock is a custom view drawn on a Canvas.
  • The Finnhub API key is kept out of the source code and read from local.properties at build time.

Interactive demo

The web demo recreates every screen in HTML and JavaScript with the same colors, rules, and formulas as the Kotlin code, so you can try the app without installing it.

Team

Ric Bryan Masagca, Paul Jazzmir Entena, Kurt Tracy Amador, and Johann Lijauco.

projects.title: Malayan Reserves
projects.summary: A campus parking reservation app: drivers see a live map of the lot, park now or book up to a week ahead, and check in on arrival, with slots released automatically when time runs out.
projects.content:
Malayan Reserves is a parking reservation app for our campus lot, made as a group project. Drivers check a live map of the lot, park in a free slot right away or book one up to a week ahead, and check in when they arrive. Our first version was a one-screen prototype that didn't build, couldn't finish a registration, and never released a slot once it was taken. I rebuilt it into a working app with a secure backend.

What it does

  • Live lot map of 12 slots in four rows, drawn like the real lot, with each parked car in its owner's color. It refreshes every 10 seconds.
  • Park now or book later: pick 1 to 4 hours and, for later, a day and start time. A timeline shows when the slot is already taken.
  • A real reservation lifecycle: a slot is held for 20 minutes, you check in with “I've parked”, and you can extend once or leave. Missed check-ins become no-shows and expired stays end on their own, so slots are never stuck.
  • Fair-use rules: one reservation per driver, no overlapping bookings, priority slots for faculty and staff, and advance bookings during campus hours.
  • Privacy: other drivers only see part of your plate number.

What I fixed

  • Build errors from a placeholder dependency version, a wrong import, and a misused lint library.
  • Registration that never finished because the app and server expected different responses.
  • A slot query that compared user IDs to emails, so slot details never loaded.
  • Reservations that were never cleared, and an app that marked slots reserved even when the server refused.
  • Plain-text passwords sent in URLs, a hard-coded server IP, and no database schema.

How it's built

  • Kotlin and Jetpack Compose with Material 3, a ViewModel with StateFlow, and a repository layer.
  • Demo mode runs on an on-device SQLite database with simulated drivers who arrive, leave, and book ahead.
  • A PHP and MySQL JSON API with PDO, transactions with row locks to prevent double-booking, bcrypt passwords, and hashed session tokens. I tested it end to end from the app.
  • The web demo is a JavaScript port of the same rules and screens, with a control to skip time ahead.

Team

Johann Lijauco, Mikhail David, Zei Ramirez, Austine Ang, and Angelo Ebrada.

A student project concept. It isn't an official Mapúa Malayan Colleges Laguna service, and the demo uses sample data saved in your browser.

projects.title: Network Labs
projects.summary: Two Cisco networking labs, VLSM with DHCP and RIPv2, and VLANs with VTP and inter-VLAN routing, rebuilt as an interactive map where you can inspect every device and trace pings.
projects.content:
Two Cisco Packet Tracer labs from my networking course, turned into an interactive viewer. Packet Tracer saves labs in an encrypted file, so I decoded my two files and rebuilt each network on the page: every device, cable, configuration and command I typed. Visitors can click any router, switch or PC to inspect it, or trace a ping and watch it cross switches, VLANs and routers.

Lab 1: Converging a network

  • Subnetted 172.10.0.0/16 with VLSM for LANs of 1,750, 750, 250 and 60 hosts (/21, /22, /24, /26), plus two /30 serial links.
  • Configured three Cisco 2911 routers: LAN gateways on the last usable address, and the DCE end of each serial link on the first.
  • Made each router a DHCP server for its LANs, so all 14 hosts address themselves automatically.
  • Converged the network with RIPv2 and no auto-summary, for end-to-end connectivity.

Lab 2: VTP and inter-VLAN routing

  • Created Faculty, Student and Admin VLANs and a VTP domain with a server, two clients and a transparent switch.
  • Assigned access ports per VLAN and trunked the links between switches.
  • Subnetted 192.168.0.0/20 for 500, 100 and 15 hosts (/23, /25, /27).
  • Set up router-on-a-stick with 802.1Q subinterfaces, and a DHCP pool per VLAN on the router.

How the viewer works

  • A Python script decodes the .pkt files and extracts the topology, the IOS configurations and the command history, with passwords hidden.
  • The page parses each IOS config in JavaScript: interfaces, switchport modes, VLANs, DHCP pools and RIP networks.
  • The ping tracer follows frames through access ports and trunks, picks the gateway from DHCP, and routes with tables built from the RIP configuration. Every host can reach every other host in both labs, and each simulated gateway matches the one saved in the original file.
  • Each router shows a show ip route table derived from its configuration.

The lab briefs and base topologies come from the course; the configuration is my own work.

projects.title: Pong Reimagined
projects.summary: A retro pixel arcade game where you are the ball: flap against gravity, chain perfect goals into combos, and collect coins and power-ups across endless stages.
projects.content:
Pong Reimagined flips Pong around: you are the ball. Gravity pulls you down, a tap makes you flap, and you have to hit the green goal on each wall to bounce back and score. Red walls and spike mines end the run.

Gameplay

  • Perfects and combos: hitting the yellow middle of a goal scores double, and three perfects in a row raise the multiplier, up to x5.
  • Coins and skins: coins collected across runs unlock seven pixel-art ball skins.
  • Power-ups: a shield that survives one hit, slow-motion, a coin magnet, and double points.
  • Close calls: passing near a mine without touching it scores a bonus.
  • Endless stages: every six goals the color theme changes and the game speeds up, adding more mines, drifting mines, and sliding goals.

How it's built

  • Plain JavaScript and Canvas with no libraries. The game draws to a real 320×180 pixel screen, scales it up at whole-number sizes so pixels stay crisp, and adds CRT scanlines.
  • All art is drawn in code from small pixel maps, so the game ships no image files.
  • All audio is synthesized with the Web Audio API, including a chiptune soundtrack that speeds up each stage.
  • Mines flash before arming and never spawn in the ball's path, verified with an automated bot over hundreds of runs.
  • An attract-mode demo plays behind the title screen, driven by the same AI used for testing.

Background

The concept comes from a game jam in October 2023, where I was the team's project manager. This version is a complete redesign with new art, sound, gameplay systems, and code.

projects.title: CLIR Book A Seat
projects.summary: A seat booking system for our school library: students see which seats are free on a live floor map and book one in two taps, while librarians manage seats, logs, and reports.
projects.content:
CLIR, the library of Mapúa Malayan Colleges Laguna, ran its Book A Seat process on Microsoft Forms and Excel. Students filled out the same long form on every visit, couldn't tell whether any seats were free before walking over, and librarians compiled usage reports by hand. Our capstone proposed a web-based booking system to fix that. This is the improved, working version of our prototype.

What it does

  • Live seat map of the Individual Study Zone (seats C-01 to C-49) showing available, reserved, occupied, on-break, and out-of-service seats, with a live count of free seats anyone can check without signing in.
  • Two-tap booking: students create an account once, so reserving a seat is just picking it and a duration. That addresses our goal of cutting check-in input by 80%.
  • Seats for your needs: filter by power outlet, window view, quiet area, private carrel, or nearness to the control desk.
  • CLIR's policies built in: up to 2 hours with one extension, a 10-minute check-in window that releases no-shows, and a visible 10-minute break timer. The timer fixes a problem from our survey: students' things being moved during short breaks.
  • Librarian dashboard: live occupancy, editing any seat's status, releasing or extending seats, and clearing all reservations at closing time.
  • Logs and reports that replace the Excel workflow: searchable session logs with CSV export, plus charts for busiest hours, sessions per day, usage by department, popular seats, and no-show rates.

How it's built

  • Plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS with no frameworks, so it runs anywhere, including this static site.
  • Shared state syncs in real time between browser tabs, and each tab keeps its own sign-in. Open the student and librarian demos side by side and bookings appear instantly.
  • A simulation of students arriving, taking breaks, and leaving keeps the floor realistic, with demo tools to fast-forward time or trigger a rush hour.
  • Our original build was an ASP.NET Web Forms prototype in C#. This version turns its static pages into a working system based on the requirements from our study: interviews with CLIR staff and a survey of 30 students.

Team

Johann Lijauco, Denzel Adrienne Arciaga, Kurt Tracy Amador, Rafael Mercado, and Daniela Madrasto.

A student project concept. It isn't an official MMCL system, and the demo uses sample data saved in your browser.

projects.title: Cipher Lab
projects.summary: Four classical ciphers written in Python for our Information Security course, including one of our own design, plus an interactive web version that shows every step of the math.
projects.content:
Cipher Lab started as a Python console program for our Information Security course. It implements four ciphers: Monoalphabetic, Vernam, Kamasutra, and Kamasutra the Vernam, a cipher our group designed that chains the other two together and flips letter case along the way.

What it does

  • Generates a fresh random key every session for the substitution ciphers.
  • Encrypts and decrypts while preserving upper and lower case, spaces, and punctuation.
  • Explains its work, printing each letter's numeric value, the key it lines up with, and the wrap-around math.
  • A CipherManager menu ties the four programs together into one application.

Bringing it to the web

To make the project easy to try, I ported each algorithm to JavaScript so it runs in the browser with no install. The web version keeps the same rules as the Python original, turns the console explanations into step-by-step tables, and shows the original Python source beside each cipher.

writing.title: Life Gave me a Lemon 🍋
writing.content:
One Monday morning, when I awoke on my bed,
A lemon fell suddenly on my head.
A strange look this lemon had, not of the usual kind,
It had an ethereal beauty to it, incomprehensible by my mind.


I quickly got up and grabbed the lemon from where it fell,
My nostrils got flooded by an aroma, an otherworldly smell.
I saw a pool from where I took it, it must have bled from the drop,
But inspecting it closer, it was cleaner than a well-polished countertop.


My curiosity piqued, and tasted a fingertips worth;
By God! No such flavor given me this much mirth.
Instinct took over me at that very instant, I must have more!
So hastily I went to the other side of my bedroom door.


In the kitchen, I grabbed the sharpest thing that's in store,
Everything that I needed to get to its delicious core.
But my first attempt was feeble, for I did not penetrate its skin,
Not even the tiniest scratch, not a loss on its glistening sheen.


The second attempt was worse, for it made the lemon jump and roll,
Out of the kitchen, and into the hall.
So to the hall I went, and eagerly chased after it,
But the lemon was faster, out of my sight in a split.


Until I no longer had the idea of where it could possibly be,
I searched every inch of my house, everywhere that I can see.
I know it's in here with me, it must have rolled into a nook—
A nook that will be impossible to look.


After hours of my perilous search, I have decided to retreat,
For I have run out of hope, and finally conceded defeat.
But that lemon will never ever leave my head;
Its mystical aura will be with me until I'm dead.


Oh, to live with such a burden is torturing me every day,
I wish to see you one last time lemon, give me a chance to say:
That I am sorry for taking your comfort from you, I was overcome with emotion,
I hope that you forgive me and accept my desperate devotion.

writing.title: The Haunting👻
writing.content:
Once upon a dreary midnight. When the sky was void of every starlight,
Stood a half-kept manor where a young man slept.
Deep in his slumber, the young man was, dreaming of glamour,
When all of sudden, he was awoken by unwanted clamor.


"Who's there?!" The young man asked with fright.
But the only answer, was the quietness of the night.
He thought little of it, and tucked himself in.
Little does he know, that's when the hauntings begin.


It started with 2 ghouls, looming like dread from afar, and slowly get closer with every setting of our star.
Closer and closer the apparitions got, the more loud and painful became its chants of rot,
"You cannot overcome us!", "We shall be your ruin!", they said in a synchronous voice.
Slowly and surely, they took the young man's poise.


Next was a phantom, so vulnerable, so deep in its woe.
It made the young man question if it is a friend or a foe.
Friend or Foe? Who knows, for it is easily swayed by the wind.
On certain nights he's a companion, on other nights he's a fiend.


Then there was the ghost of a lovely woman in white.
Who only shows herself in his dreams every night.
Unlike the others, she does not break the young man with fright,
But taunts him with what he longs for, she tortures him with his sight


This went on for weeks then months, then years.
They tried to drive him mad, slowly draining him of his tears.
But the young man stood strong, He overcame his fears,
And gradually, he learned to live with his new peers.

writing.title: The Box 📦
writing.content:
I woke up to find a box on the sidewalk, a few feet from my door.
It had no such labels. No sender and receiver address,
only the words "Your burden will be no more.".


What could that mean? I thought while staring at the box.
It looked like it was in amazing condition.
No dents, no tears - so perfect I swore it had a glow,
It only added to my confusion.


I imagined the different items that could fit inside.
"Your burden will be no more." I keep muttering to myself as I thought,
I exhausted everything my mind could provide.


A million dollars or a bomb, A golden ticket or poison.
That was the conclusion that I came to.
Thinking of the worst made me deathly afraid to even lay a finger on the it,
I don't want to move it from its position.


Suffering or Happiness, whatever that box is offering as a solution.
I hurriedly went inside my home and locked the door behind me.
Making sure to not be affected by the box's intention.


As I never left my house for the rest of the day,
So did the thought of the box inside my head.
What if I'm missing on something big? What if I end up dead?
Questions begging to be answered, lingering on my mind as I lay.


Maybe I'm just overthinking it, I thought, my courage starting to grow.
I got up from my bed and opened the door. What's inside the box!? You might be wondering.
I guess we'll never know.


For when I stepped outside, the box was no longer there.
I wondered where it went, when I heard my neighbor.
Bursting with joy. "Thank Jove for this box!" I heard them say.
"We are set for life!", those words echo in my mind every single day.


I wish I had enough courage
I wish I just had enough care.
But it's all too late now - all I could do is just stare.
